abstract: The conversion of CO2 into carbon-based fuels via electrochemical reduction is a promising approach to realizing the termination of carbon cycling. Copper (Cu 0 ) is considered to be an effective electrochemical catalyst for such purpose. However, it is limited by its instability and low selectivity. In this work, Cu 2+ was embedded into a polycondensation structure of resorcinol (R) and formaldehyde (F) via sol-gel reaction, and the complex was then calcined at high temperature to obtain copper nanoparticles-dispersed carbon aerogels (Cu/CA). The samples were further activated sequentially under CO2 and N2 atmosphere. The final products under different activation temperature of secondary N2 atmosphere were obtained and marked as Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T. The existence of highly dispersed Cu 0 on the carbon aerogels was confirmed by XPS and HRTEM, which exhibited attractive activity towards electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) forming carbon product in 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous media. Furthermore, the CO2RR product distribution varied under different samples. The sample activated under 700°C (Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700) with Cu loading c.a. 5.13 wt% showed remarkable CO faradaic efficiency (FE) (75.6%) at low overpotential of -0.49V. Further calcination led to more exposure of copper, and CO dimerization to C2 product. The high selectivity toward CO by Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 maybe attributed to their excellent stability in maintaining the metallic nature of Cu component within the hydrophobic carbon aerogels during electrocatalysis, which further prevents the adsorption and reduction of CO on the catalyst.

Abstract The conversion of CO2 into carbon-based fuels via electrochemical reduction is a promising approach to realizing the termination of carbon cycling. Copper (Cu 0 ) is considered to be an effective electrochemical catalyst for such purpose. However, it is limited by its instability and low selectivity. In this work, Cu 2+ was embedded into a polycondensation structure of resorcinol (R) and formaldehyde (F) via sol-gel reaction, and the complex was then calcined at high temperature to obtain copper nanoparticles-dispersed carbon aerogels (Cu/CA). The samples were further activated sequentially under CO2 and N2 atmosphere. The final products under different activation temperature of secondary N2 atmosphere were obtained and marked as Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T. The existence of highly dispersed Cu 0 on the carbon aerogels was confirmed by XPS and HRTEM, which exhibited attractive activity towards electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) forming carbon product in 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous media. Furthermore, the CO2RR product distribution varied under different samples. The sample activated under 700℃ (Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700) with Cu loading c.a. 5.13 wt% showed remarkable CO faradaic efficiency (FE) (75.6%) at low overpotential of -0.49V. Further calcination led to more exposure of copper, and CO dimerization to C2 product. The high selectivity toward CO by Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 maybe attributed to their excellent stability in maintaining the metallic nature of Cu component within the hydrophobic carbon aerogels during electrocatalysis, which further prevents the adsorption and reduction of CO on the catalyst.
Keywords: CO2 electrochemical reduction; Cu nanoparticles; carbon aerogel; CO2 activation; N2 activation
1. Introduction
Recently, the concentration of atmospheric CO2 has risen continuously due to accelerated burning of fossil fuel, resulting in the increase of global average temperature and sea levels, melting of large-scale ice and snow, which threatens the living environment of mankind[1, 2]. The dual pressure of environmental crisis and energy crisis has aroused great attention to the recycling of CO2. To carbon neutrality, using electrochemical method to convert CO2 into chemical fuel is a superior approach [3-5]. Unfortunately, the strongly stable chemical bond in CO2 (C= O, 806 kJ mol −1 ) and the competing reaction, especially hydrogen evolution reaction ( HER) in the aqueous phase will lead the quite inefficient electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR)[6]. Among all catalyst materials, gold and silver have been known as the most efficient electrochemical catalyst, but their high cost limits their applications[7-11]. Consequently, the abundant non-precious metals and carbon nanostructure materials have been investigated to replace silver and gold based catalysts[12, 13]. Metal Cu-based catalysts are extensively studied owing to their capability of catalyzing the conversion of CO2 with very high efficiency[14, 15]. In earlier works, Cu foil was directly used as the catalyst of electrochemical reduction of CO2. With the advancement in nanoparticles (NPs) synthesis, Cu nanocatalysts have demonstrated superior activity and selectivity for CO2 reduction. Recently, the study of Cu-based catalysts mainly focused on Cu NP shape[16, 17], Cu NP size[18-20], Cu-alloy[21-23], Cu-based core/shell[24, 25], Cu NP catalysis[26, 27], and Cu nanoporous catalysts[28-30]. However, only a few Cu-based catalysts are adequate for reducing CO2 to advanced hydrocarbons and oxygenates. Furthermore, faradaic efficiency (FE) was varied depending on the catalyst preparation techniques. SpeciallyCu 0 is easily deactivated and oxidized at room temperature, which hampers its electrocatalytic development. Sen et. al[31]synthesized hierarchical porous Cu nanofoam, which helped to produce HCOOH and CO with FE of 37% and 10%, respectively. Cu alloyed with another metal (AuCu, CuPt) could stabilize Cu NPs for efficient CO2RR and
contribute to CO, CH4 with the FE less than 45%[22, 32]. Carbon black[23], carbon nanotubes[33] and graphene[34] were also used to stabilize Cu NPs during CO2RR. In recent time, carbon aerogels have been investigated for electrocatalysis because they possess distinct advantages in terms of active sites and increased specific surface area[35]. Furthermore, the hydrophobic surface of aerogel may repel water and inhibit the H2 reaction whilst the porous structure may faciliatate the diffusion of CO2 across the gas-liquid interface. However, there are few reports on the aerogel-stabilized metals, especially copper NPs for CO2RR.
Herein, we focus on exploring a novel synthesis method of copper NPs-dispersed carbon aerogels for CO2RR. Resorcinol and formaldehyde were used as RF resin precursors and copper acetate as catalyst. After sol, gel, aging, displacing, freeze-drying, and carbonization, carbon aerogel stabilized copper nanoparticles were obtained. Further activation under CO2 and N2 calcination was explored to obtain porous structure. Influence of temperature of secondary N2 activation was explored for better efficiency of electrochemical reduction of CO2 in KHCO3 solution. Since copper salt was added as catalyst, its final amount of Cu 0 was limited, and hence the final activity of CO2RR, yet its enhanced activity stabilized by porous carbon aerogel still illuminated the application of Cu in the field of electrocatalytic CO2RR.
2. Experiments
In a typical process, copper carbon aerogel was prepared by dissolving resorcinol(R) and formaldehyde (F) (molar ratio 1:2) in deionized water (20 mL) and adding a small amount of copper acetate (0.05 moL) as catalyst. The mixture was stirred until a homogenous solution was obtained. A trace amount of Na2CO3 was then added as a blowing agent, after which the resulting mixture was subjected to ultrasonic treatment for half an hour. The solution was sealed into ampoules and placed in a blast air oven at 45 ℃ for 24 h and then 90℃ for 72 h. The hydrogels formed were immersed in acetone bath for 3 days which was displaced by fresh acetone every day. The organic aerogel was
carbonized at 600℃ for 2 h, then heated to 760℃ for 2 h at a heating rate of 5℃ min -1
under N2 flow. The sample was cooled at room temperature and then thermal
activation was carried out in a flow of CO2 at 850 ℃ for 2 h. The product was marked as Cu/Ac-CO2. Finally, the Cu/CA-CO2 was heated to an appointed temperature(T) under N2 flow. The corresponding samples were labelled as Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T (T=650, 700, 750, 800, 900 ℃).
2.2 Electrochemical measurement
Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) measurements were carried out in a gas-tight two-compartment electrochemical cell, which was separated by Nafion 117 membrane. Glassy carbon electrode, Pt electrode and Ag/AgCl electrode were used as the working electrode, counter electrode and reference electrode, respectively. All potentials measured with an Ag / AgCl reference electrode was converted to the RHE reference scale by the formula E (vs. RHE) = E (vs. Ag/AgCl) + 0.21 V + 0.0591pH.
5 mg sample was dispersed in 63 L of ethanol and 88 L of DMF. 25 L of nation solution was added and the solution was sonicated for 1 hour to form a uniform solution. 10 L of the solution was dropped on the glassy carbon electrode. The gas products of CO2RR were monitored by a micro gas chromatography (GC) (Agilent 490) equipped with a TCD detector and Molsieve 5A column once every thirty minutes.

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
An illustration of the synthesis process for the Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T is shown in Fig. 1. In
the typical reaction, it is desired to fix Cu 2+ into the three-dimensional framework formed by the polycondensation of RF. In addition, the hydrogen bond in the solution also contributes strong connection between RF and Cu 2+ [36, 37]. After the curing step, certain amount stable Cu 2+ embedded into xerogel structure can be obtained[38]. Then, the sample was then freeze-dried, further carbonization, and further activated sequentially under CO2 and N2 to obtain 3D aerogel with uniformly distributed Cu NPs.
Fig.1 Schematic illustration of the synthesis of Cu/Ac-CO2-N2-T
Fig. 2a illustrates the SEM image of Cu/Ac. The 3D microspheres were shown with uniformly distributed copper nanoparticles after freeze-drying and carbonization under N2 atmosphere. The morphology of Cu / Ac is comprised of large joined spheres with diameters of about 500 nm with metal particles of about 20-30 nm homogeneously dispersed in the surface of spheres. The HRTEM image (Fig. 2e) indicated that copper NPs were well crystalline and the calculated lattice constants (0.208nm) were corresponding to the interplanar spacing of the crystal face of copper. The d002 spacing of 0.335 nm is characteristic of graphitic carbon. The interconnected structure indicated the existence of synergistic effect, facilitating the enhanced catalytic activity. The elemental mapping images of

3.2 Electrochemical performance analysis of catalysts for CO2 reduction To elucidate the influence of the secondary activation of N2 and determine the optimal Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T preparation conditions, Cu/CA-CO2 were activated at a range of temperatures under N2 atmosphere (650-900℃), and were subsequently assessed for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction. The CO2 reduction activity of Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T was evaluated using cyclic voltammetry(CV) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) in an H-cell filled with CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution with a standard three-electrode configuration(Fig 3S).
Fig. 4 (a) LSV curves of Cu/CA-CO2 -N2-700 on glassy carbon electrodes in N2- or CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution at the scan rate of 10 mV s -1 ; (b) LSV curves of the Cu/CA-CO2 -N2-T catalyst on glassy carbon electrodes in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution at the scan rate of 10 mV s −1 ; (c) Chronoamperometric curves of stability test with Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 at -0.60 V versus RHE in the CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution.
During electrochemical CO2 reduction process, one major challenge is the simultaneous evolution of hydrogen (HER, hydrogen evolution reaction). Therefore, the target for electrochemical CO2 reduction is to increase CO2 reduction activity and inhibit
hydrogen evolution, and a reasonable designed catalyst is needed[18]. As shown in Fig. 4a, the reduction activity of three catalysts (Cu/CA, Cu/CA-CO2, Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700) was evaluated by comparing the onset potential in N2 saturated solution and CO2 saturated solution, respectively. All samples exhibited obvious responses to CO2 with lower onset potential in CO2 as compared to N2. This suggested a better CO2RR activity compared to HER activity. The CO2 reduction onset potential of the Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 was about 397 mV lower than the onset potential of hydrogen production. The CO2RR onset potential of Cu/CA-CO2 was about 245 mV lower than onset potential of HER, while Cu/CA was only about 22 mV lower. The result indicated that Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 had higher activity for CO2 reduction and could highly suppress HER very well. Fig. 4b illustrated the LSV curves of Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T samples in CO2-saturated 0.1M KHCO3 aqueous solution, among which the Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 catalyst exhibited the lowest onset potential. At -0.6V (versus RHE), the current density of Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 reached c.a. 5 mA cm -2
, much higher than those of Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T (T=650, 750, 800,
900℃). The stability of the Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 was shown in Fig. 4c. A negligible reduction current decay was shown during a 10 h test at -0.60 V versus RHE, illustrating its excellent long-term stability during electrochemical reduction CO2.
The CO2 saturated KHCO3 solution was electrolyzed in a potentiostatic mode to quantify the selectivity and activity of Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T towards CO2RR. The entire process was continuously kept at a constant flow rate of CO2 of 30 mL min -1 , and the cathode chamber outlet was connected to a gas chromatograph (GC) to quantitatively analyze the gas phase product. The liquid product of the electrochemical reduction of CO2 was quantitatively analyzed by 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. To obtain insight into the relevant catalytic pathways of CO2RR, faradaic selectivity measurements were performed under stationary reaction conditions at −0.6 V/RHE. The electrochemical CO2RR production distribution and corresponding Faraday Efficiency (FE) under different samples are listed in Table 1. As indicated, there was
multicomponent distribution under different samples, including CO, CH4, C2H4, C2H6, HCOOH, and H2.

As a comparison, CV of Cu/CA, Cu/CA-CO2, and Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 under
different scan rate was carried out in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution, and the scan rate versus current density at -0.4V was plotted to obtain the specific capacitance of different samples (Fig. S4). The specific capacitance of Cu/CA, Cu/CA-CO2, and Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 was 18.5mF cm -2 , 145.7mF cm -2 , and 196.5mF cm -2 respectively, suggesting a high electrochemical active surface area (Fig. 5b). The result is consistent with their surface area of Cu/CA (201.8 m 2 g -1 ), Cu/CA-CO2(665.1 m 2 g -1 ), and Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700(867.8 m 2 g -1 ), indicating higher surface area could facilitate active center scattering. Fig.5b illustrated the scan rate versus current density at -0.4 V of Cu/CA-CO2-N2-T to obtain active surface area. Cu/CA-CO2-N2-650 exhibited the highest electrochemical active surface area of 234.1mF cm -2 , which corresponded to its high FE of H2. Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 showed moderate specific capacitance (196.05 mF cm -2 ). There was decreased specific capacitance with increasing temperature except for Cu/CA-CO2-N2-750 (196.06 mF cm -2 ). Cu/CA-CO2-N2-800(132.23 mF cm -2 ) and Cu/CA-CO2-N2-900(128.50 mF cm -2 ) had lower specific capacitance hence the lower FE of CO, but higher C2 production, mainly due to their high BET surface area, i.e, Cu/CA-CO2-N2-800(901.7 m 2 g -1 ) and Cu/CA-CO2-N2-900(913.5 m 2 g -1 ). The Raman spectra of the samples at various activation temperatures are shown in Fig. S5. The
intensity ratio of the D and G bands (ID / IG) can be used to indicate the density of defects in the carbon aerogel[41, 42]. The change in defect density is one of the factors affecting the catalytic activity of the material. At temperature of 700℃, the ID / IG value is 1.25. The higher defect density lead to higher activity and its hydrophobicity and increased pore size and pore volume of the aerogel makes CO2 mass transport easier at lower potentials[43]. It also facilitates CO* intermediates transporation, and easy desorption to form CO[44]. As the activation temperature rises, the ID / IG value decreases leading to decreased defect density. With the pore size and pore volume of the sample decrease, the diffusion of *CO intermediate is blocked which results in concentrated *CO coverage leading to C2 selectivity but decreased FE of CO (Fig. 6)[45, 46]. As to the Cu/CA-CO2-N2-650, its flocculent structure and lower contact angle lead to decreased CO2 activity, but it has higher surface area and higher specific capacitance, which facilitate HER activity (Fig. S6)
Conclusions In summary, we explored an environmentally friendly and effective approach for the
synthesis of copper nanoparticles dispersed carbon aerogels. Enhanced electrochemical reduction of CO2 in 0.1 M KHCO3 after Cu/CA activated under CO2 and N2 gas flow was achieved. The samples were activated in an N2 atmosphere under different temperatures (900 ℃, 800℃, 750℃, 700℃, 650℃) to explore its influence on electrochemical reduction of CO2. Electrochemical measurements revealed that Cu/CA-CO2-N2-900, Cu/CA-CO2-N2-800, Cu/CA-CO2-N2-750 demonstrated better activity towards the generation of C2 hydrocarbons. Most importantly, Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 with Cu loading of 5.13 wt% demonstrated an impressive activity of electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO (FE=75.6%), and a long-term stability (10 h). Cu/CA-CO2-N2-700 had a high specific surface area (867.87m 2 g -1 ), largest pore size (2.36 nm), moderate specific capacitance (196.05 mF cm -2 ) and contact angle of 113°, which could contribute to its high activity of CO2 reduction. Since the copper amount is low, enhanced weight ratio of Cu and
atom-dispersed Cu was still under exploring to further widen the application of copper dispersed-carbon aerogel.
